name: Alacatlatzala Mixtec
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Zylstra, Carol F. 1980. Phonology and morphophonemics of the Mixtec of Alacatlazala, Guerrero. SIL-Mexico Workpapers 4: 15-42. (scan)
catalog_locator: Sec. 1 'Syllable, couplet, phonological word', p.16; Rule 9 'Stress Shift', p.28; fn.3, pp.37-38; sec. 4 tones, p.22 ('There are three tonemes: high, mid, and low'); p.24 rules preamble listing the feature stress [str].
catalog_quote: [p.16] The phonological word is composed of a stem (two or three syllables) and its prefixes, suffixes and enclitics. It is defined as a sequence of syllables which can be spoken in isolation and which has only one stress. Stress falls on the initial syllable of the couplet except for the stress shift to the second syllable of the couplet when followed by the first person postclitic -ì (5.2).³ Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a three-syllable stem. ... For example, a three-syllable transitive verb stem may occur with as many as two aspect prefixes and both subject and object enclitics, as in the word šìnàsa'náʔaràñá "already he taught her." Stress (') falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem sa'náʔa. [p.28, Rule 9. Stress Shift.] When the first person singular clitic -ì is added to a stem the stress shifts to the last syllable of the stem. ... /kìsi-ì/: kì'si-ì "my cooking pot" /veʔe-ì/: ve'ʔe-ì "my house" [fn.3, p.37] It is difficult to hear any stress differentiation on couplets in isolation. Couplets of the CVʔV pattern appear to have extra force on the syllable beginning with glottal stop. Couplets of the other CV patterns appear to have equal stress on each syllable. The stress on the first syllable of the couplet is more prominent phonetically when the couplet is surrounded by prefixes and/or postclitics. ... Because of the behavior of stress in the longer words it is reasonable to assume that the lexical stress is on the first syllable of the couplet.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Zylstra, Carol F. 1980. Phonology and morphophonemics of the Mixtec of Alacatlazala, Guerrero. SIL-Mexico Workpapers 4: 15-42.
new_statements.locator: Section 1 'Syllable, couplet, phonological word', p. 16 (p. 2); footnote 3, p. 37 (p. 23); Rule 9 'Stress Shift', p. 28 (p. 14)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (image-only, 28 pp = journal pp. 15-42) plus its scanned. I rendered p.2 (= p.16) and p.23 (= p.37) as page scan and read them directly. The quoted passage is on p.16 exactly as reported: 'The phonological word is composed of a stem (two or three syllables) and its prefixes, suffixes and enclitics. It is defined as a sequence of syllables which can be spoken in isolation and which has only one stress. Stress falls on the initial syllable of the couplet except for the stress shift to the second syllable of the couplet when followed by the first person postclitic -i (5.2).3 Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a three-syllable stem.' The page continues with the 7-syllable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per phonological word, located on the stem: the first syllable of the disyllabic couplet (root), i.e. the penultimate syllable of the stem; in trisyllabic stems the penultimate syllable. Prefixes and enclitics do not carry or attract stress, except that the 1sg enclitic -ì shifts stress to the couplet's final syllable. The language also has three phonemic level tones, independent of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Footnote 3 notes that in isolation CVʔV couplets seem to have extra force on the glottal-stop syllable and other couplets sound evenly stressed; stress on the couplet-initial syllable becomes clearly audible when prefixes/enclitics surround the couplet.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the second (last) syllable of the couplet/stem when the first person singular postclitic -ì is added (Rule 9, p. 28: kì'si-ì 'my cooking pot', ve'ʔe-ì 'my house'). Monosyllabic proclitic particles (či 'because', nda 'from', ta 'and') are normally unstressed but take the stress of a separate phonological word when the host word already has the seven-syllable maximum (p. 16).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem plus prefixes, suffixes, enclitics, 1-7 syllables), defined as having exactly one stress; stress is computed on the stem/couplet, not from the word edge including clitics. Author cautions stress is hard to hear on isolated couplets (citation forms) and is clearest in affixed words.
new_statements.identity_note: Zylstra 1980 describes the Mixtec of the town of Alacatlazala (her spelling), Municipio de Malinaltepec, Guerrero, data from one 17-year-old native speaker (Juan Galindo Cano); this is exactly Glottolog alac1244 / ISO mim. She notes it is 'largely mutually unintelligible' with Metlatónoc Mixtec (Overholt 1961 = metl1238), which is a different variety.

new_statements.quote: The clitic i causes the stress to shift to the final syllable of the stem.

For details of the phonology.. see Zylstra (1980)'; no defa…
new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing Zylstra 1980 statement (stress on the initial syllable of the couplet, with a stress shift before enclitic i); adds nothing new on default placement, restates the clitic-i stress-shift exception and the prestressed/poststressed pronoun terminology. Live SIL URL is 404; obtained archived copy (Internet Archive, 20 Jun 2012) by automated download -4; image-only PDF, scanned at 300 dpi one page at a time.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The sketch has no stress section (0.2 Phonology lists consonants, vowels and three surface tones high/mid/low and refers to Zylstra 1980 for phonology). Its one stress statement is the exception: the 1sg enclitic i shifts stress to the final syllable of the (disyllabic) stem, which presupposes default stress on the non-final, i.e. first syllable of the stem couplet = penult of the bare stem; third-person clitic pronouns are classed as 'prestressed' vs 'poststressed' by position relative to the stressed stem. The default placement itself is not stated here, hence low confidence for the placement label; the work is a tone description plus this stress-shift rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the stem-final syllable before the first person singular enclitic i (same as Zylstra 1980 Rule 9 'Stress Shift'); enclitic un instead nasalizes/retunes the stem-final vowel without a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Zylstra 1991 sec. 0.1: the variety is that of Alacatlatzala village (municipio Malinaltepec, Guerrero), mutually intelligible with Atlamajalcingo del Monte, Coatzoquitengo, Tototepec, Mixtecapan and other neighbouring towns; data from three young men of Alacatlatzala. The maize vocabulary is likewise 'mixteco de Alacatlatzala, municipio de Malinaltepec, Guerrero' (mim). Both are alac1244.

tone_statements.quote: Las lenguas mixtecas son tonales. Hay tres tonos básicos en el to̱ꞌon sávi: alto, medio y bajo. El tono alto se escribe con un acento agudo sobre la vocal, como en la primera vocal de xáko ‘tlacuache’. El tono bajo se escribe con una raya debajo de la vocal, como en la primera vocal de ki̱si ‘olla’. El tono medio no se representa con tilde alguna... El tono en sí marca la diferencia entre ciertas palabras, como ño̱ꞌon ‘sol’ de ñoꞌo̱n ‘lumbre’, pero también indica los tiempos del verbo en muchos casos...
tone_statements.translation: The Mixtec languages are tonal. There are three basic tones in to̱ꞌon sávi: high, mid and low. High tone is written with an acute accent over the vowel, as on the first vowel of xáko 'opossum'. Low tone is written with a line under the vowel, as on the first vowel of ki̱si 'pot'. Mid tone is not represented with any mark... Tone by itself marks the difference between certain words, such as ño̱ꞌon 'sun' vs ñoꞌo̱n 'fire', but it also indicates verb tenses in many cases...
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3 'Tonos', pp. 4-5; restated in Apéndice B p. 10 ('Se utilizan tres tonos: alto, medio y bajo.')
tone_statements.summary: Orthography guide: three level tones (high, mid, low), lexically and grammatically (verb tense) contrastive; each vowel of a long (double) vowel may carry its own tone (p. 4). Nothing on word stress.

sources.note: Reconstructs Proto-Mixtec with two tone registers (high, low) plus a 'modified' sandhi tone and couplet-final glottal stop, i.e. basic couplets *high-high('), *low-low('), *low-high, *high-low (Chart 2, p. 22).
